name: Jazz — New Orleans
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: New Orleans, Louisiana — the Mississippi port city where jazz was born around 1900. T1: New Orleans is the home of jazz; brass bands parade the streets and mourners dance behind the coffin at a jazz funeral in a moving crowd called the 'second line' (answer: the second line). T2: In Congo Square, enslaved Africans were allowed to gather on Sundays to drum and dance — the one place in the U.S. where African rhythms openly survived, seeding jazz (answer: Congo Square). T3: Storyville, the city's red-light district (1897–1917), gave early pianists like Jelly Roll Morton steady work; when the Navy closed it in 1917, musicians rode the riverboats up to Chicago (answer: Storyville). T4: Louis 'Satchmo' Armstrong, born in New Orleans in 1901, turned jazz from group playing into the art of the improvising SOLOIST and popularized 'scat' singing (answer: Louis Armstrong). T5: Buddy Bolden, a New Orleans cornet player around 1900, is remembered as the first 'king' of the loud improvised 'hot' sound — but no recording of him survives, so his music is legend (answer: Buddy Bolden). Deeper rungs: the cornet/trumpet lead, Dixieland collective improvisation, Mardi Gras Indians, Preservation Hall, the 'cradle not sole origin' caveat.
source: Wikipedia 'Jazz', 'Congo Square', 'Storyville, New Orleans', 'Louis Armstrong', 'Buddy Bolden'; Grokipedia (intended primary — Grokipedia WebFetch returned 403 and WebSearch budget was exhausted this session, so verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — open on a street parade or a jazz funeral, never 'What is jazz?'; invert the wonder (the dancing crowd behind the coffin → 'the second line'). Dinner-test payoff = Congo Square (the one American place enslaved people could keep African drumming) and the Buddy Bolden 'no recording survives' legend rung — label Bolden's sound as remembered/legendary, and frame New Orleans as jazz's cradle, not its sole origin. LANE BORDER: New Orleans food (gumbo, beignets) belongs to the COOKING bank — a one-line scene mention is fine, but every answer here is the MUSIC/place.

name: The Blues — the Mississippi Delta
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: The Mississippi Delta — the flat cotton floodplain between the Yazoo and Mississippi rivers where the blues took shape ~1900–1920s. T1: The Delta blues is played on a guitar with a glass or metal slide ('bottleneck') worn on a finger, making the string 'cry' like a human voice (answer: slide/bottleneck guitar). T2: Dockery Farms, a cotton plantation near Cleveland, Mississippi, is often called the birthplace of the blues because Charley Patton and other founders lived and played there (answer: Dockery Farms). T3: At the crossroads of Highways 61 and 49 in Clarksdale, legend says guitarist Robert Johnson sold his soul to the devil at midnight for his talent (answer: the crossroads legend). T4: In 1903 bandleader W.C. Handy, waiting at the Tutwiler train station, heard a man press a knife against his guitar strings and sing about 'goin' where the Southern cross the Dog' — the first blues he ever heard (answer: W.C. Handy at Tutwiler station). T5: The Delta's simplest instrument, the one-string 'diddley bow' nailed to a porch wall, taught many bluesmen their first notes and shaped the slide sound (answer: the diddley bow). Deeper rungs: the 12-bar form, 'Highway 61' the Blues Highway, field-holler call-and-response, the Great Migration carrying the blues to Chicago.
source: Wikipedia 'Delta blues' (verified this session: Mississippi Delta origin, slide-guitar hallmark, Patton recorded 1929–30, Johnson recorded 1936–37); Wikipedia 'Dockery Farms', 'Robert Johnson', 'W.C. Handy' (autobiography 'Father of the Blues', Tutwiler 1903); Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a knife on guitar strings at a lonely train platform, never 'What is the blues?'; invert (the eerie crying-guitar sound → 'the slide'). ACCURACY RAIL: label as LEGEND the crossroads/soul story (folklore, not fact) and Dockery as 'often called' the birthplace (a claim). Dinner-test payoff = the crossroads legend and the porch-wall diddley bow. LANE BORDER: keep answers on the music/place; the Great Migration is carried as light place-culture backdrop, not a history-bank episode.

name: Hip-hop — the Bronx
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: The West Bronx, New York City — where hip-hop was born at a 1973 rec-room party. T1: On August 11, 1973, in the rec room of 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, DJ Kool Herc spun records at his sister Cindy Campbell's back-to-school party — the event most often called the birth of hip-hop (answer: 1520 Sedgwick Avenue). T2: Herc noticed dancers went wildest during the drum 'break' of a song, so he used two copies of the same record to loop that break forever — the 'breakbeat' (answer: the break/breakbeat). T3: The dancers who saved their best moves for the break became 'b-boys' and 'b-girls' doing a new floor dance — breaking (answer: breaking/b-boying). T4: Grandmaster Flash, another Bronx DJ, perfected cutting between two turntables exactly on the beat ('quick-mix theory'), and Grand Wizzard Theodore invented the scratch (answer: Grandmaster Flash / the scratch). T5: Afrika Bambaataa turned Bronx gang energy into the Universal Zulu Nation and named hip-hop's 'four elements': DJing, MCing (rapping), breaking, and graffiti (answer: the four elements). Deeper rungs: Coke La Rock as an early MC, the park jams / plugging turntables into a lamppost, 1970s Bronx decay as backdrop, the 'one of several birthplaces' caveat.
source: Wikipedia '1520 Sedgwick Avenue' (verified this session: Aug 11 1973, DJ Kool Herc / Cindy Campbell party, extended breaks, described as 'one of the pivotal and formative events' — not sole origin); Wikipedia 'Hip hop', 'Grandmaster Flash', 'Afrika Bambaataa'; Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a summer rec-room party with two turntables, never 'What is hip-hop?'; invert (dancers exploding at one moment of a song → 'the break'). ACCURACY RAIL: 1520 Sedgwick is the most-credited birthplace, but hip-hop 'developed slowly in several places in the 1970s' — frame it as THE famous origin party, not the sole one. Dinner-test payoff = the break discovery (two copies of one record looped forever) and DJs plugging turntables into a Bronx lamppost for park jams. LANE BORDER: keep every answer the music/place.

name: The Tango — the Río de la Plata (Buenos Aires & Montevideo)
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: The dockside barrios of Buenos Aires (Argentina) and Montevideo (Uruguay), on opposite banks of the Río de la Plata, where tango was born in the 1880s. T1: Tango was born in the crowded immigrant docklands of Buenos Aires AND Montevideo, on the two banks of the Río de la Plata — so both Argentina and Uruguay claim it (answer: the Río de la Plata / both cities). T2: The soul of tango is the bandoneón, a square button 'accordion' — but it was invented in GERMANY (by Heinrich Band) and carried to the docks by immigrants (answer: the bandoneón). T3: Carlos Gardel, the golden-voiced singer who died in a 1935 plane crash, made the tango-song ('tango-canción') world-famous; Argentines say 'Gardel sings better every day' (answer: Carlos Gardel). T4: 'La Cumparsita,' the most famous tango in the world, was written in 1917 by a Uruguayan student, Gerardo Matos Rodríguez, in Montevideo (answer: La Cumparsita). T5: In 2009 UNESCO put tango on its heritage list as a JOINT treasure of Argentina AND Uruguay — a rare shared listing that settled the two nations' rivalry over it (answer: the joint Argentina–Uruguay UNESCO listing). Deeper rungs: the close embrace, the milonga (dance hall), the compadrito and the arrabal, Ástor Piazzolla's 'nuevo tango'.
source: Wikipedia 'Tango' (verified this session: 1880s Río de la Plata origin; UNESCO inscribed 31 Aug 2009 as a joint Argentina+Uruguay proposal); Wikipedia 'Bandoneon' (German origin, Heinrich Band), 'Carlos Gardel', 'La Cumparsita'; Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — immigrant dockworkers dancing in a Río de la Plata port, never 'What is tango?'; invert (a heartbreak-sounding instrument at the docks → 'the bandoneón'). ACCURACY RAILS: the bandoneón is GERMAN (not Argentine), and tango is a SHARED Argentine–Uruguayan creation (both banks) — don't hand it to Argentina alone. Dinner-test payoff = the German-bandoneón surprise and the 2009 joint UNESCO listing that split the honor between two countries. LANE BORDER: keep answers on the music/place; the great immigration wave is place-culture backdrop, not a history-bank episode.

name: Flamenco — Andalusia
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: Andalusia (Andalucía), southern Spain — where flamenco grew from Roma, Moorish, Jewish, and Andalusian roots. T1: Flamenco was born in Andalusia among the Roma ('gitanos'), blending the sounds of Moorish, Jewish, and Andalusian Spain into one fiery art (answer: Andalusia / the gitanos). T2: A full flamenco has three parts — the singing (cante), the dancing (baile), and the guitar (toque) — and the crowd drives it with rhythmic hand-claps called palmas (answer: cante/baile/toque + palmas). T3: The heartbeat of flamenco is the compás — a demanding 12-beat rhythmic cycle that the clapping, guitar, and heel-stamps must all lock into (answer: the compás). T4: Poet Federico García Lorca gave a name to flamenco's dark, goosebump-raising soul: duende, the spirit that arrives only when a performer risks everything (answer: duende). T5: The wooden box-drum you now see in flamenco, the cajón, is NOT Spanish — Paco de Lucía brought it back from PERU in the 1970s and it became standard (answer: the cajón). Deeper rungs: the palos (soleá, bulerías, seguiriya, alegrías), Triana/Jerez/Cádiz heartlands, the zapateado footwork and bata de cola dress, UNESCO 2010.
source: Wikipedia 'Flamenco', 'Cajón' (Peruvian origin, adopted via Paco de Lucía), 'Duende (art)'; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription (2010); Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a clapping crowd and a stamping dancer in an Andalusian courtyard, never 'What is flamenco?'; invert (the goosebump-soul a singer summons → 'duende'). ACCURACY RAILS: name the multi-culture confluence honestly (Roma + Moorish/Al-Andalus + Sephardic Jewish + Andalusian folk); the cajón is a PERUVIAN import (1970s), not native. Dinner-test payoff = duende and the Peruvian-cajón surprise. LANE BORDER: no tapas/sherry/food answers — those are the COOKING bank; every answer is the MUSIC/place.

name: Samba & Bossa Nova — Rio de Janeiro
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — the 'Marvelous City' that birthed samba, then bossa nova. T1: Samba was born among Afro-Brazilian communities in Rio and now powers Carnival, where rival 'samba schools' (escolas de samba) parade for the crown (answer: samba / the samba schools). T2: Rio built a special half-mile stadium just for the Carnival parade — the Sambadrome (Sambódromo), designed by Oscar Niemeyer and opened in 1984 (answer: the Sambadrome). T3: A samba band's secret weapon is the cuíca, a friction drum rubbed with a wet stick to make a high 'laughing/monkey' squeak (answer: the cuíca). T4: In the late 1950s, in the beach neighborhood of Ipanema, João Gilberto and Antônio Carlos Jobim slowed samba into the cool, whispering bossa nova (answer: bossa nova / Ipanema). T5: 'The Girl from Ipanema' (1962), written by Jobim and Vinícius de Moraes about a real girl walking to Ipanema beach, became one of the most-recorded songs ever (answer: The Girl from Ipanema). Deeper rungs: the surdo/tamborim/agogô, batucada, the morros/favelas as samba's cradle, 'Pelo Telefone' (1917) as an early recorded samba.
source: Wikipedia 'Samba', 'Bossa nova', 'Sambadrome Marquês de Sapucaí' (Niemeyer, 1984), 'The Girl from Ipanema'; Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a thundering Carnival parade or a quiet Ipanema beach bar, never 'What is samba?'; invert (a stadium built only for a parade → 'the Sambadrome'; a drum that laughs → 'the cuíca'). ACCURACY RAIL: samba's roots are Afro-Brazilian (Bahian migrants to Rio) — name that honestly; bossa nova is a 1950s offshoot, not a separate origin. Dinner-test payoff = the cuíca's laughing squeak and the real Girl from Ipanema. LANE BORDER: no feijoada/caipirinha/food answers (COOKING bank); Christ the Redeemer and Sugarloaf are scene-setting only — every answer is the MUSIC.

name: Reggae, Ska & Dub — Kingston, Jamaica
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: Kingston, Jamaica — the small city that invented ska, rocksteady, reggae, dub, and dancehall. T1: Jamaican music runs on the 'sound system' — a giant mobile stack of speakers that DJs wheeled into Kingston yards to throw street dances in the 1950s (answer: the sound system). T2: Around independence in 1962, Kingston sped up American R&B and put the accent on the OFF-beat, creating the bouncy sound of ska (answer: ska). T3: In Trench Town, a poor Kingston neighborhood, Bob Marley and the Wailers turned the slower 'one drop' beat into reggae, the sound that carried Rastafari worldwide (answer: reggae / Trench Town). T4: In a Kingston studio, engineer King Tubby stripped the vocals off a record and remixed the bass-and-drum 'riddim' into an echoing instrumental — inventing dub, the ancestor of the remix (answer: dub / King Tubby). T5: In 1985 the all-electronic 'Sleng Teng' riddim launched digital dancehall — and one computer beat got reused on hundreds of records (answer: dancehall / the Sleng Teng riddim). Deeper rungs: rocksteady (~1966), Studio One 'the Jamaican Motown', Lee 'Scratch' Perry, the toasting DJ as ancestor of rap, UNESCO reggae 2018.
source: Wikipedia 'Reggae', 'Ska', 'Dub music', 'Sound system (Jamaican)', 'Sleng Teng'; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage reggae inscription (2018); Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a wall of speakers in a Kingston yard, never 'What is reggae?'; invert (a record with the singing stripped off, all echo and bass → 'dub'). ACCURACY RAIL: keep the chain in order (sound system → ska → rocksteady → reggae → dub → dancehall); Rastafari is described, not evaluated. Dinner-test payoff = dub as the birth of the remix (King Tubby erasing the vocals) and one Sleng Teng beat reused everywhere. LANE BORDER: keep answers on the music/place; Rastafari and Marcus Garvey stay light context, not a history-bank episode.

name: The Steel Pan — Trinidad
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: Trinidad and Tobago — birthplace of the steelpan ('pan'), built from oil drums. T1: The steelpan, Trinidad's national instrument, is played on the hammered end of a discarded 55-gallon oil drum — a whole orchestra made from oil barrels (answer: the steel pan / oil drum). T2: When colonial rulers banned African skin drums in the 1880s, Trinidadians drummed on tuned bamboo stalks instead — the 'tamboo bamboo' bands that came before pan (answer: tamboo bamboo). T3: Around WWII, empty oil drums piled up near Trinidad's refineries and U.S. bases; players hammered dents into the ends and found each dent could be tuned to a different note (answer: the oil drum / tuning the dents). T4: Every Carnival, steelbands battle in a fierce competition called Panorama, arranging one tune for a hundred pans (answer: Panorama). T5: In 1951 the Trinidad All-Steel Percussion Orchestra (TASPO) took pan to the Festival of Britain in London, proving the 'dustbin' instrument was a real orchestra (answer: TASPO / 1951). Deeper rungs: calypso and its descendant soca as the music pan plays; the 'kaiso' calypso wars; Winston 'Spree' Simon and Ellie Mannette; the ping-pong/tenor pan.
source: Wikipedia 'Steelpan' (verified this session: tamboo bamboo predecessor, 1880s skin-drum ban after the 1881 Canboulay riots, oil drums ~1937/1947, TASPO Festival of Britain 26 Jul 1951, Winston 'Spree' Simon, Ellie Mannette 'Father of the Modern Steel Drum'); Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a Carnival band making music on hammered oil barrels, never 'What is a steelpan?'; invert (a discarded oil drum → a tuned instrument). ACCURACY RAIL: the pan is often called 'the only acoustic instrument invented in the 20th century' — present that as a widely-repeated CLAIM, and lean on the solid dated facts (skin-drum ban, oil drums, TASPO 1951). Dinner-test payoff = an orchestra built from garbage oil drums. LANE BORDER: keep answers the INSTRUMENT/tradition.
history_overlap: The 1880s colonial skin-drum ban / 1881 Canboulay riots could duplicate a Caribbean-colonial history episode; keep this rung's answer the Trinidad instrument and tamboo-bamboo tradition, not the political event.

name: Mariachi — Jalisco, Mexico
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: The state of Jalisco, western Mexico — cradle of mariachi. T1: The mariachi, Mexico's serenading band in silver-buttoned charro suits, comes from the state of Jalisco (answer: Jalisco). T2: The small Jalisco town of Cocula is called the 'cradle of mariachi,' where the son jalisciense folk style took shape (answer: Cocula). T3: A mariachi's rhythm comes from two guitars you won't see elsewhere: the small high-pitched vihuela and the huge, deep-bellied bass guitarrón (answer: the vihuela and guitarrón). T4: The blaring trumpet everyone thinks is ancient was only added to mariachi in the 1930s, pushed by Mexican radio (answer: the trumpet — added in the 1930s). T5: In 2011 UNESCO named mariachi an Intangible Cultural Heritage of humanity; in Mexico City, mariachis wait for hire every night in Plaza Garibaldi (answer: UNESCO 2011 / Plaza Garibaldi). Deeper rungs: the traje de charro suit, 'Cielito Lindo' / 'El Son de la Negra', the grito shout.
source: Wikipedia 'Mariachi' (Jalisco/Cocula cradle, vihuela + guitarrón, trumpet added 1930s); UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription (2011); Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a silver-buttoned band serenading in a Jalisco plaza, never 'What is mariachi?'; invert (a huge fat-bellied bass guitar → 'the guitarrón'). ACCURACY RAIL: the trumpet is a 1930s ADDITION, not original — a clean myth-bust. Dinner-test payoff = the modern trumpet surprise and the giant guitarrón. LANE BORDER: tequila (Jalisco's agave spirit) is a COOKING/food answer — keep every answer the MUSIC/place.

name: The Waltz — Vienna
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: Vienna, Austria — where the waltz swept into the ballrooms and scandalized Europe. T1: The waltz, the spinning ballroom dance of 1800s Vienna, shocked polite society because the man held the woman in a CLOSE embrace as they turned — thought scandalous at the time (answer: the close embrace). T2: The waltz grew out of a stomping Austrian and Bavarian peasant dance called the Ländler, cleaned up for the city ballroom (answer: the Ländler). T3: Johann Strauss II, the 'Waltz King' of Vienna, wrote hundreds of waltzes and ruled the city's ballrooms (answer: Johann Strauss II). T4: Strauss's 'By the Beautiful Blue Danube' (1866) became Vienna's unofficial anthem — named for the great river that curves past the city (answer: The Blue Danube). T5: At the 1814–15 Congress of Vienna, so much dancing filled the diplomacy that a prince quipped 'the Congress dances, but does not advance' (answer: the Congress of Vienna). Deeper rungs: the Vienna New Year's Concert tradition, the fast 'Wiener Walzer', the whirling turn.
source: Wikipedia 'Waltz', 'Ländler', 'Johann Strauss II', 'The Blue Danube', 'Congress of Vienna'; Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a whirling Viennese ballroom that scandalized onlookers, never 'What is a waltz?'; invert (the shocking part of the dance → 'the close embrace'). ACCURACY RAIL: the 'scandalous' reaction is the documented period response (close hold + fast turning were thought improper) — state it as historical reaction, not a modern verdict. Dinner-test payoff = the closed-embrace scandal and 'the Congress dances, but does not advance.' LANE BORDER: keep answers the dance/place.
history_overlap: The Congress of Vienna rung is a light place-anchored aside; if the history bank owns the Congress as a diplomacy episode, keep this answer the DANCING-at-the-Congress detail, not the treaty settlement.

name: Fado — Lisbon
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: Lisbon, Portugal — home of fado, the 'song of longing.' T1: In the old Lisbon quarters of Alfama and Mouraria, a singer in a black shawl pours out fado — a music built on one deep, bittersweet feeling of longing (answer: fado / Lisbon). T2: That feeling has a special Portuguese name with no English equal: saudade, a yearning for someone or something loved and lost (answer: saudade). T3: Fado is carried by a unique instrument, the guitarra portuguesa — a pear-shaped, 12-string guitar that shimmers and cries (answer: the guitarra portuguesa). T4: Amália Rodrigues, the 'Queen of Fado,' carried Lisbon's song to the world in the 20th century; when she died in 1999 Portugal declared national mourning (answer: Amália Rodrigues). T5: In 2011 UNESCO recognized Lisbon's fado as Intangible Cultural Heritage; legend traces it to Maria Severa, a 19th-century Lisbon singer (answer: UNESCO 2011 / Maria Severa). Deeper rungs: Coimbra fado (university, male students) vs Lisbon fado, the tasca/fado house, the black mourning dress.
source: Wikipedia 'Fado', 'Guitarra portuguesa', 'Amália Rodrigues', 'Maria Severa'; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription (2011); Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a shawled singer in a candlelit Alfama tavern, never 'What is fado?'; invert (an untranslatable Portuguese ache → 'saudade'). ACCURACY RAIL: label the Maria Severa origin as legend/tradition; saudade is described in the scene, never dropped as a rote dictionary definition. Dinner-test payoff = saudade (a feeling English can't name) and the crying 12-string guitarra. LANE BORDER: keep answers the music/place.

name: Kabuki & Noh — Japan
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: Japan — home of Noh and Kabuki, two of the world's oldest living theatres. T1: Kabuki, Japan's flashy, colorful theatre, was started around 1603 by a WOMAN — a shrine dancer named Izumo no Okuni — performing on a dry riverbed in Kyoto (answer: Izumo no Okuni / Kyoto). T2: Women were soon banned from the stage, so ALL kabuki roles — including the female ones — became played by men; a male actor specializing in women's roles is an onnagata (answer: the onnagata / all-male casts). T3: Kabuki actors freeze at a dramatic peak in a bold cross-eyed pose called the mie, and wear vivid painted-line makeup called kumadori (red lines for a hero, blue for a villain) (answer: the mie / kumadori). T4: Kabuki stages have a raised walkway, the hanamichi, that runs right through the audience so actors make grand entrances among the crowd (answer: the hanamichi). T5: Noh, Japan's OLDER theatre (perfected by Zeami in the 1300s), is the opposite of kabuki — slow, hushed, and performed behind carved wooden masks (answer: Noh / the masks). Deeper rungs: the shamisen accompaniment, Bunraku puppet theatre, the revolving stage (a Japanese invention).
source: Wikipedia 'Kabuki' (verified this session: 1603 Izumo no Okuni on the Kyoto riverbed, women banned 1629, onnagata, hanamichi, kumadori red/blue, mie, shamisen); Wikipedia 'Noh', 'Zeami Motokiyo'; Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a painted actor freezing mid-pose on a runway through the crowd, never 'What is kabuki?'; invert (the theatre a woman founded that then banned women → Okuni + the onnagata). ACCURACY RAIL: kabuki was FOUNDED by a woman and then became all-male — keep that surprising sequence exact; Noh is the older, slower, masked form. Dinner-test payoff = a woman inventing the all-male theatre, and the cross-eyed mie freeze. LANE BORDER: keep answers the performing-art/place.

name: The Gamelan — Java & Bali
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: The islands of Java and Bali, Indonesia — home of the gamelan bronze orchestra. T1: A gamelan, the shimmering orchestra of Java and Bali, is made almost entirely of tuned BRONZE — gongs and metal-key instruments struck with mallets (answer: bronze gongs/metallophones). T2: A gamelan is tuned to ITSELF, not to a world standard, so two gamelans can't swap players — and each set uses one of two scales, sléndro or pélog (answer: sléndro & pélog / self-tuning). T3: The whole ensemble is anchored by one enormous gong, the gong ageng, whose deep boom marks the end of each musical cycle (answer: the gong ageng). T4: In Bali, two players hammer out lightning-fast interlocking parts — kotekan — so quick that together they sound like one impossible melody (answer: kotekan). T5: Gamelan and firelight accompany wayang kulit, all-night shadow-puppet plays where a single puppeteer voices every character behind a screen (answer: wayang kulit). Optional deeper rung (label carefully): the Balinese kecak 'monkey chant,' a chorus of chanting men, was shaped in the 1930s from an older trance ritual (with artist Walter Spies).
source: Wikipedia 'Gamelan' (verified this session: Javanese/Balinese bronze ensemble, sléndro & pélog tuning, gong ageng, kotekan, self-tuning, wayang kulit); Wikipedia 'Kecak', 'Wayang kulit'; Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a shimmering bronze orchestra behind a shadow-puppet screen, never 'What is a gamelan?'; invert (an orchestra that can't share players with any other → self-tuning, sléndro/pélog). ACCURACY RAIL: teach 'metallophone' and the two scale names before testing them; if the kecak rung is used, label it a 1930s creation drawn from an older ritual (not ancient). Dinner-test payoff = a self-tuned bronze orchestra and the all-night shadow-puppet play. LANE BORDER: keep answers the music/place.

name: Throat-Singing — Tuva & Mongolia
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: Tuva (southern Siberia) and Mongolia — the steppe homeland of overtone throat-singing. T1: On the grasslands of Tuva and Mongolia, herders sing so that ONE person makes two or more pitches at the same time — throat-singing, or khöömei (answer: throat-singing / khöömei). T2: The trick is physics: the singer holds one low droning note and shapes mouth and throat to amplify a faint high 'overtone' above it, like a whistle riding the drone (answer: amplifying an overtone/harmonic). T3: Different shapes make different styles — the high piercing whistle is sygyt; the deep growling rumble is kargyraa (answer: sygyt & kargyraa). T4: Throat-singers say they are imitating their LAND — the whistle of steppe wind, the burble of a river, a bird's call echoing off a cliff (answer: imitating the natural soundscape). T5: In 2010 UNESCO recognized Mongolian khöömei as Intangible Cultural Heritage of humanity, protecting a sound tied to nomadic herding life (answer: UNESCO 2010). Deeper rungs: the igil / morin khuur (horsehead fiddle) accompaniment, the animist bond to nature, the Altai mountains.
source: Wikipedia 'Tuvan throat singing', 'Khoomei', 'Overtone singing'; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage Mongolian khöömei inscription (2010); Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — a lone herder on the steppe making two notes at once, never 'What is throat-singing?'; invert (one singer, two pitches → amplifying an overtone). ACCURACY RAIL: the two-pitch effect is real acoustics (amplifying a harmonic overtone above a droned fundamental), not a trick or myth — explain the harmonic before naming the styles. Dinner-test payoff = one voice becoming two pitches, and the singing that copies wind and rivers. LANE BORDER: the birds/animals imitated are scene, not biology — the answer is the vocal technique/place, never the creature's anatomy (that's the ANIMAL bank).

name: The Bagpipes' Contested Home
strand: Music & dance born in a place
scope: The bagpipe — claimed by Scotland, but far older and more widespread than that. T1: Everyone pictures the bagpipe as Scottish (the loud Great Highland Bagpipe IS Scotland's national instrument) — but the bagpipe is NOT originally Scottish (answer: not originally Scottish / a myth). T2: A bagpipe is really a clever machine: a bag of air the player squeezes, a melody pipe (the chanter), and constant humming 'drone' pipes — and versions exist all across Europe and the Middle East (answer: the bag + chanter + drones / it's pan-European). T3: Ireland has its own gentler indoor pipes filled by a BELLOWS squeezed under the elbow, not blown by the mouth — the uilleann ('elbow') pipes (answer: the uilleann pipes). Optional deeper rung: cousins across Europe — the Galician gaita, the Breton biniou, the Bulgarian gaida.
source: Wikipedia 'Bagpipes', 'Great Highland bagpipe', 'Uilleann pipes'; Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
framing_note: Scene-led — the surprise that the 'most Scottish' sound isn't Scottish in origin; invert (the world's most stereotyped-Scottish instrument → actually ancient and pan-European). ACCURACY RAIL: label the origin as CONTESTED/ancient (references appear in Roman and Near-Eastern sources; there is no single inventor-nation) — do NOT assert a false single birthplace. The Great Highland Bagpipe being Scotland's national instrument is true and separate from the instrument's deep origin. Dinner-test payoff = the bagpipe is not really Scottish.
